title: North Side Canal Company rehabs aging canals near Milner Dam to curb major water loss in Magic Valley - Idaho News 6
summary: North Side Canal Company rehabs aging canals near Milner Dam to curb major water loss in Magic Valley Idaho News 6
text:
MURTAUGH, Idaho — Ask people about the biggest issues facing the Magic Valley, and water is likely near the top of the list. It's the backbone of the local economy, supporting agriculture, businesses and everyday life.
Near Milner Dam, the North Side Canal Company is working to rehabilitate its canals and cut down on the amount of water that essentially slips through the cracks every summer.
The irrigation season is over, but Alan Hansten with the North Side Canal Company told me there's plenty of work to get done in the off season.
Hansten said 50 to 60 percent of water in the canal system is lost through either seepage out through the porous sides of the canal, or through evaporation.
"The contractors that built the canal originally had to come in and line it with concrete so the concrete has degraded over the last hundred years; it's starting to crumble and fall apart and we need to come back in and reline the section of canals," Hansten said.
For the next few weeks, crews will be spraying new concrete lining on 4,000 feet of the canal. This is the second phase of the project to fully re-coat a total of 8,000 feet of its mainline canal at Milner Dam.
With a dry 2026 and high anxiety about next year's irrigation season, canal companies like North Side are looking for ways to increase efficiency to get the most out of what water is available.
"Back in the day when they blasted this channel out, they put the water into it to deliver to the farmers, and the water went down into the cracks and down to the ground, essentially returning back to the river. We weren't able to get it on beyond this location, so this section needs to be lined in order to keep the water flowing to the farmers here on the north side," Hansten said.
Rehab of this section will cost a combined $9 million, split between a grant and a loan from the Idaho Board of Water Resources.
"We live in a desert; there's no economy in Idaho if you don't have water," Idaho Board of Water Resources member Brian Olmstead said.
Olmstead said a lot of things about water have changed, including how much Mother Nature provides.
"There's aging infrastructure that's failing on virtually every canal in the state," Olmstead said.
"So we're improving the canal system, so irrigation gets more efficient more of it's going into the crop unless of it into the ground," Olmstead said.

text:
Idaho Legislature may clamp down on high powered e-motorbikes amid injuries
The exterior of the Idaho Statehouse as seen on March 16, 2026, in Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun)
Two Idaho lawmakers from Ada County are teaming up to introduce a bill to regulate high powered e-motorbikes, citing an uptick injuries.
Rep. Brooke Green, a Boise Democrat, and Sen. Treg Bernt, a Meridian Republican, on Thursday announced they plan to introduce a bill during the upcoming legislative session to require so-called e-motos — which they say can reach over 30 mph but are often marketed as e-bikes — to be classified as motorcycles. That change would require riders of e-motos to have a driver’s license with a motorcycle endorsement to ride on public roads, and for the vehicles to meet certain requirements to be considered street legal, the lawmakers say.
Since the start of the year, Idaho emergency rooms have seen nearly 1,900 visits due to electric mobility devices, a category that also includes e-bikes and e-scooters, according to data from the Idaho Department of Health and Welfare. Young boys, between the ages of 11 and 15, accounted for 306 of the visits — the most of any demographic reported. An Idaho Statesman report published earlier Thursday highlighted the spike in injuries.
“Families are spending thousands of dollars on what they believe are bicycles, without realizing their 14-year-old cannot legally ride them down Eagle Road or on the Greenbelt,” Bernt and Green said in a joint statement. “Kids are getting seriously hurt, and we need to address this before more injuries occur.”
Ahead of the holiday season, the lawmakers urged parents to not buy e-motos for children who can’t legally drive motorcycles on public roads.
The proposed statewide change seems similar to an action the city of Boise took earlier this year.
Other cities have taken notice, too.
Meridian in July launched an education campaign focused on the use of e-bikes and e-motorcycles, BoiseDev reported. Nampa in September passed an ordinance adding local regulations, including barring e-motos from sidewalks and greenbelts if they can reach speeds in excess of 28 miles per hour, the Idaho Statesman reported.
“There’s nothing wrong with enjoying these vehicles in the desert or on our public lands where motorized recreation is permitted, but motorcycles do not belong on the Greenbelt, sidewalks, or other pedestrian spaces,” the lawmakers added. “We want parents to have the facts before making expensive holiday purchases, and we’re working on bipartisan legislation to establish clear rules that keep our communities safe.”
